newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DIARY - DUTCH POLITICS WEEK OF AUGUST 18.
newsitem.headline: DIARY - DUTCH POLITICS WEEK OF AUGUST 18.

text.p: Last cabinet members return
from summer recess. Extra cabinet meetings have been scheduled
to discuss the budget which is to be presented on September 16.
Parliament continues summer recess until August 25.
These are some of the main topics which dominated Dutch
politics last week:
1,500 Dutch troops take part in military exercises with
Polish troops in Poland from August 16.
BUDGET: Prime Minister Wim Kok says a tax windfall of
between 3.5 and four billion guilders is expected in 1998. It
has not yet been decided how this extra money is to be spent.
Following the first cabinet meeting after the summer recess, Kok
also said the government was working on broadening the tax
system after the year 2000, in order to lower rates.
ASYLUM: The Lower House says it will respect a Hague court
ruling that the Iranian Nasseri family, who were refused asylum,
may be sent back to Iran. The coalition parties do, however,
want a hearing regarding the human rights situation in Iran. The
Netherlands regards Iran as a so-called safe country for the
return of refugees. Prior to the court's ruling, father Majid
Nasseri went on a hunger strike, claiming he is a political
refugee and that his life would be in danger if he was to return
to Iran.
AVIATION: Transport minister Annemarie Jorritsma is to
implement drastic measures to curb noise pollution at Schiphol
Airport. From September 1, an independent coordinator will
determine the number of flights to be allowed at the Amsterdam
airport. Last week, a Haarlem court ruled that only the
minister, not Schiphol, could take measures to reduce the noise,
particularly at night.
MAAS RIVER: The Liberal and Christian Democratic parties
criticise the Transport and Water Affairs minister's plan to
delay for ten years the deepening and broadening of the Maas
river in the province of Limburg. The two billion guilder
project to safeguard the area during floods, was to have been
completed by 2005.
DRUGS: Health minister Els Borst is willing to fund
research into the medical benefits of marijuana. Earlier this
month, she banned doctors and pharmacists from prescribing the
soft drug, due to the lack of proof of the benefits in existing
scientific research. Patients suffering from aids and MS claim
marijuana helps against pain.
The Lower House regards as too large the planned experiment
by the Health ministry to provide hard drugs to 750 heroine
addicts. Minister Borst wants to implement the programme, based
on the Swiss model, in an attempt to re-integrate long-term
heroine users into society.
